title: Jeep Wrangler Unlimited (LJ)
verdict: The LJ is a TJ that went to the gym and grew ten inches of wheelbase, which turned out to be exactly the right number. Jeep sold it for barely two and a half model years and buyers mostly shrugged. Now everyone wants one, and the sellers know it.

paragraphs: In April 2004, eighteen years after the [[jeep/cj-8|CJ-8 Scrambler]] went away, Jeep brought back a long-wheelbase Wrangler. It stretched the [[jeep/tj|TJ]] by 10 inches between the axles and about 15 inches overall, and called it the Wrangler Unlimited. Owners call it the LJ. That gave a two-door Wrangler 2 more inches of rear legroom, 13 more inches of cargo space and a tow rating of 3,500 lb instead of 2,000. It sold for $24,995 at launch and lasted barely two and a half model years. Then it became one of the most chased Wranglers ever built.

story.heading: THE SCRAMBLER'S WHEELBASE, RETURNED
paragraphs: The LJ's 103.4-inch wheelbase is almost exactly the 103.5 inches of the [[jeep/cj-8|CJ-8 Scrambler]] it was reviving. The longer frame gets one extra crossmember, and the body grows behind the rear wheels. That stretch is why the rear overhang is the LJ's one real off-road compromise: Jalopnik's David Tracy lists a 27.7-degree departure angle, and the low transfer-case skid makes the belly the next thing to touch.

Mechanically it is a late TJ. The engine is the 4.0-liter AMC-derived straight six, rated at 190 hp and 235 lb-ft. Standard LJs got a Dana 44 rear axle with a 3.73 limited-slip and the Command-Trac NV231 transfer case with a 2.72:1 low range. The standard short-wheelbase TJ made do with a Dana 35 unless you ticked the right option boxes. Automatics used the 42RLE four-speed, and Jeep's 2004½ spec sheet lists only that automatic for the first LJs. For 2005, manual Wranglers moved from the NV3550 five-speed to the six-speed NSG370.

story.heading: THE RUBICON UNLIMITED
paragraphs: For 2005, Jeep gave the long-wheelbase body the Rubicon drivetrain. The Rubicon Unlimited had Dana 44 axles at both ends with air-actuated lockers, the Rock-Trac NV241 transfer case with a 4:1 low range, 4.10 gears (Jeep's spec sheet says 4.11), diamond-plate rocker guards and LT245/75R16 Goodyear MT/R tires. You could have it with the six-speed manual or the four-speed automatic.

Jeep also built 1,000 numbered 'Sahara Edition' Unlimited Rubicons in 2005 to cash in on the film Sahara. All were Light Khaki, with a chrome grille, khaki tops, graphite Moab wheels, two-tone seats and a numbered dash badge. In Jalopnik's breakdown, the Rubicon LJ is the one that puts the whole formula together: TJ coil springs, a fully boxed frame and a wheelbase in the trail 'sweet spot', plus a factory locker on each axle.

story.heading: WHY COLLECTORS CHASE THEM
paragraphs: Jalopnik, citing forum and sales data, puts LJ production at about 47,000 over the run, roughly 20 percent of Wrangler sales in those years. That isn't rare by Jeep standards. What made them collectible is that the LJ has no direct replacement. In 2007 the [[jeep/jk-unlimited|JK Unlimited]] grew four doors, a 116-inch wheelbase and about 350 more pounds. The LJ is still the only factory Wrangler that combines two doors, a long wheelbase, a coil-sprung solid-axle chassis and the 4.0 straight six.

Hagerty's valuation team says later TJs, 'and especially the Unlimited Rubicon, have been the priciest TJ on the market.' Jalopnik called the LJ the 'holy grail' of Jeeps. Unrusted, unmodified examples now command a clear premium over short-wheelbase TJs, while a clapped-out one is still just a TJ with more frame to rot.

story.heading: HOW IT ENDED
paragraphs: The TJ family finished with the 2006 model year. Its replacements debuted at the January 2006 Detroit show. The [[jeep/jk|JK]] two-door kept a short wheelbase, and the [[jeep/jk-unlimited|JK Unlimited]] replaced the LJ with four doors and a wheelbase about 13 inches longer again. The long two-door Wrangler was never offered again, and the TJ and LJ were the last Wranglers with the AMC-derived 4.0 straight six.

callout.label: SIDEBAR · THE FIVE-DOOR COUSIN
callout.title: Israel built the LJ that Jeep wouldn't
paragraphs: From 2006 the Israeli firm Automotive Industries Ltd. built the M-242 Storm Mark II under licence from Chrysler for the Israel Defense Forces, based on the TJ. Unlike any civilian Wrangler of the time, it had rear passenger doors, which makes it the first five-door Wrangler derivative.

The Storm II stretched the wheelbase to 2,931 mm, almost exactly the 116 inches Jeep would later use for the four-door [[jeep/jk-unlimited|JK Unlimited]]. In other words, the military answer to 'what comes after the LJ' arrived before Jeep's own.

engineering_intro: Underneath, the LJ is a TJ with a longer ladder frame (fully boxed, according to the Jeep engineer Jalopnik interviewed) and one extra crossmember. It has coil springs and live axles at both ends, located by four links and a track bar at each end, and recirculating-ball steering. Every LJ got the stronger Dana 44 rear axle. Rubicon Unlimiteds add a Dana 44 front axle, air lockers and a 4:1 transfer case.

engineering.note: 10 in longer than the 93.4 in TJ, with one extra crossmember. About 167 in long, or 171 in with the spare.
Leading arms and a track bar in front, trailing arms and a track bar at the rear, with stabilizer bars and gas-charged shocks at both ends (Jeep's 2004½ spec sheet).
190 hp at 4,600 rpm and 235 lb-ft at 3,200 rpm. Cast-iron block and head, 6 qt of oil.
The 42RLE has an overdrive lockout switch on the dash. Manual TJs used the NV3550 five-speed through 2004.
Both part-time with no center differential. Rock-Trac only on the 2005–06 Rubicon Unlimited.
Standard LJs: limited-slip 3.73 rear. Rubicon: air lockers front and rear with 4.10 gears.

generations_table.note: Launched April 2004 at $24,995. Dana 44 limited-slip rear (3.73), NV231 transfer case; Jeep's 2004½ spec sheet lists the 42RLE automatic.
NSG370 six-speed replaces the five-speed manual. Watch for OPDA wear on 2005–06 engines.
Dana 44 front and rear with air lockers, 4:1 Rock-Trac, 4.10 gears, LT245/75R16 MT/Rs, diamond-plate rockers.
1,000 numbered, all Light Khaki, tied to the film Sahara. Manual and automatic versions.
93.4 in wheelbase, 2,000 lb tow rating, Dana 35 rear on many trims. See the TJ page.

buying_checks.head: Get under it with a flashlight and a hammer
buying_checks.body: Quadratec calls frame rot near the rear lower control-arm brackets 'the TJ issue'. The other early-rot zones are the transfer-case crossmember area and the central body mounts. A clean outside means nothing. Probe the inside of the rails and the arm brackets, and walk away from anything that's flaking through.

buying_checks.head: 2005–06: ask about the OPDA
buying_checks.body: Late 4.0 engines can wear out the oil pump drive assembly. Owners describe the warning noise as a 'laughing monkey' squeal. Quadratec says that if there's no record of it being replaced or updated, deal with it proactively.

buying_checks.head: Is it a real Rubicon Unlimited?
buying_checks.body: Rubicons have a Dana 44 front axle, an NV241 Rock-Trac transfer case, air lockers and 4.10 gears. Check that both lockers engage, that 4-Low is the 4:1 Rock-Trac, and that a Sahara Edition has its numbered dash badge. Rubicon decals are cheap; Dana 44 fronts are not.

buying_checks.head: Drive it at 30–50 mph over bumps
buying_checks.body: OffroadXtreme suggests testing for death wobble in that speed range. A loose lower track-bar bolt, bent steering linkage, worn ball joints or tie-rod ends can all start it. On lifted examples, also check the rear track-bar bracket on the axle for cracks.

buying_checks.head: Look for leaks, and price them
buying_checks.body: The 4.0 commonly seeps from the rear main seal, oil pan, valve cover and oil-filter adapter gasket. Pinion and transfer-case output seals weep too. Mostly this is money rather than doom, but the rear main seal is a big job.

buying_checks.head: Check the radiator tanks
buying_checks.body: Factory TJ radiators have plastic end tanks crimped to an aluminum core. Quadratec says many start leaking at the upper seams around 100,000 miles. Look for green crust and a coolant smell.

buying_checks.head: Shift into 4-Low, twice
buying_checks.body: The factory 'Z-bar' transfer-case linkage pops out of worn plastic bushings, and the symptom is a Jeep that won't go into 4-Low. The bushings are cheap; a missed diagnosis is not.

buying_checks.head: Judge the modifications
buying_checks.body: A lifted LJ needs a longer or adjustable track bar, alignment correction and often a slip-yoke eliminator above 2 inches of lift. Ask who did the work, and inspect welds on frame repairs and brackets.

repairs.title: Replace the oil pump drive assembly (2005–06 4.0)
repairs.cost: Parts plus labor; ExtremeTerrain rates the install 'difficult' and suggests a professional
repairs.symptoms: A squeak or 'laughing monkey' chirp from the back of the engine, sometimes with a check-engine light. Left alone, Quadratec warns, OPDA failure can damage the engine.
repairs.fix: The OPDA sits in the block where a distributor would be. It drives the oil pump and carries the camshaft position sensor, so it must go in with the engine at top dead centre on cylinder 1 and be indexed so the cam sensor stays in sync with the crank. Follow the factory service manual's alignment procedure. Remove the cam sensor, unbolt the hold-down and lift the old drive out. Fit the replacement with a new gasket at the same orientation, then check cam/crank sync with a scan tool. ExtremeTerrain says the factory unit's two bronze bushings sit either side of a seal that starves the upper bushing of oil, and the redesigned part moves the seal above the top bushing.
repairs.tools: Socket set · factory service manual for TDC and indexing · scan tool to verify cam/crank sync · new camshaft position sensor (5149034AA for 2005–06 4.0) if the old one is suspect.

parts.name: Crown Automotive oil pump drive, 2005–06 4.0 L TJ
Crown Automotive 5149034AA camshaft position sensor, 2005–06 TJ & Unlimited 4.0
Mopar J3172332 oil pump gasket, 2001–06 TJ

repairs.title: Repair rotted rear control-arm frame mounts
repairs.cost: Frame sections plus welding; Quadratec calls shop cost 'prohibitive' for an old Jeep
repairs.symptoms: Flaking, swollen or holed frame around the rear lower control-arm brackets, the transfer-case crossmember or the central body mounts. Quadratec's correspondent found all three on a 1998 TJ with 190,000 miles.
repairs.fix: Only for someone who can cut and weld. Support the frame on stands, jack the axle, then unbolt the upper and lower control arms on one side, the sway-bar link and, if needed, the shock. Mark at least 1 inch of overlap and cut out the rotten section and the old arm mounts, without cutting the body mount and keeping clear of brake and fuel lines. Mock up the new section, grind to bare metal, measure, tack, measure again, then weld it fully. Prime and coat it, and refit the arms with thread locker and correct torque. Re-check after a day, or a mile, and then monthly. One side at a time.
repairs.tools: Welder · cutoff wheel and grinder · jack stands · floor jack · torque wrench · thread locker · rust-proof coating. Rust Buster sections are side- and year-specific (2003–06 differ from 1997–02).

parts.name: Rust Buster full center frame with trail-arm mount, 2003–06 TJ (left)
Rust Buster full center frame with trail-arm mount, 2003–06 TJ (right)
Rust Buster center frame skid-plate mount, 2003–06 TJ

repairs.title: Hunt down death wobble and set toe in the driveway
repairs.time: An afternoon to diagnose; minutes to set toe
repairs.cost: Usually a track-bar bushing, tie-rod end or ball joints, plus an alignment
repairs.symptoms: Violent front-end shake after a bump, usually at 45–65 mph, that stops only when you slow right down.
repairs.fix: Start at the front track bar. With the Jeep on the ground, have a helper rock the steering wheel a quarter turn each way while you watch both track-bar ends and the bracket holes; any side-to-side movement is a fault. Then check the tie-rod ends, drag link, ball joints, control-arm bushings, wheel bearings and tire balance. Quadratec says a steering stabilizer rarely fixes the cause. Replace the worn part and re-torque the front-end hardware. Set toe-in by loosening the tie-rod sleeves and turning the tie rod until the front of the tires is about 1/16 inch (no more than 1/8 inch) closer than the rear. Center the wheel with the drag-link turnbuckle, then get a proper alignment.
repairs.tools: 13 mm and 15 mm sockets · tape measure · pipe wrench or locking pliers · a helper · torque wrench.

parts.name: Crown Automotive 52088431 front track-bar bushing, TJ & Unlimited
Crown Automotive RT21017 adjustable front track bar, TJ & Unlimited
Crown Automotive RT21008 heavy-duty steering stabilizer, TJ & Unlimited

repairs.title: Replace the radiator before the plastic tank lets go
repairs.symptoms: Coolant smell, green crust or seepage at the upper tank seam, often around 100,000 miles, and creeping temperatures on the trail. OffroadXtreme notes that the 4.0 runs hot and recommends an all-aluminum radiator.
repairs.fix: With the engine cold, drain the coolant and remove the upper and lower hoses. On automatics, disconnect the transmission cooler lines and cap them. Unbolt the fan shroud and lift it back over the fan, then remove the radiator mounts and lift the radiator out. Transfer any brackets, fit the new radiator and shroud, reconnect everything, refill and bleed the air out with the heater on high. Buy the right radiator for your transmission: Griffin's ExactFit listed here is for manual-transmission Jeeps, and CSF's 3426 is specific to 2005–06.
repairs.tools: Drain pan · pliers for the hose clamps · line wrench for the cooler lines · funnel · coolant to the spec on the cap and in the owner's manual.

parts.name: Griffin 5-00032 ExactFit aluminum radiator, 1987–06 YJ/TJ/Unlimited (manual trans)
Fairchild MCH1064 upper radiator hose, TJ 4.0

repairs.title: Replace a throttle position or crank sensor
repairs.symptoms: Stalling, rough idle or random check-engine lights. Quadratec's example was a TJ throwing P0122 that stalled while driving; automatics rely on the TPS to run properly. Aging crankshaft-position, throttle-position and oxygen sensors are all common failures.
repairs.fix: For the TPS: disconnect the negative battery terminal, then unplug the TPS, IAC motor and MAP sensor connectors. Remove the intake tube and unclip the throttle cable (plus the kickdown and cruise cables where fitted). Remove the four throttle-body bolts, take the TPS off with a T25 Torx, fit the new sensor with the supplied hardware, and refit the throttle body, replacing the gasket if it's tired. For a crank sensor, Mopar's 4727451AA is listed for 2003–06 4.0 TJs.
repairs.tools: 13 mm (or 1/2 in) socket for the battery · 5/16 in driver · 10 mm socket · T25 Torx · code reader.

parts.name: Mopar 4727451AA crankshaft position sensor, 2003–11 TJ 4.0 & JK 3.8

repairs.title: Fix a transfer case that won't go into 4-Low
repairs.cost: A few dollars in bushings, or an adjustable linkage
repairs.symptoms: The lever moves but the transfer case won't fully engage 4-Low, or pops out of it. Quadratec says the factory 'Z-bar' linkage pops out of worn plastic bushings.
repairs.fix: Put the lever in neutral, chock the wheels and crawl under. Pry the linkage rod ends off the shifter and transfer-case arms, replace the worn plastic bushings, and snap the linkage back on. If the Z-bar is bent or the geometry has changed after a lift, fit an adjustable linkage and set it so the lever fully reaches every detent. Then test 4-Hi, N and 4-Lo with the engine running.
repairs.tools: Flat screwdriver or trim tool · pliers · wheel chocks.

parts.name: Lynx adjustable transfer-case shifter linkage, 1997–06 TJ
TJ transfer-case shifter linkage and brackets

repairs.title: Replace a front axle U-joint and unit bearing
repairs.symptoms: A squeak that fades as speed rises, a vibration or bind on slow turns as if you were in 4WD, and visible play in the axle-shaft U-joint. Quadratec's correspondent found the hub was worn too once it was apart.
repairs.fix: Jack up the axle and remove the wheel. Remove the two caliper bolts and hang the caliper so it isn't supported by the brake hose, then pull the rotor. Stop the hub from turning and break the 36 mm axle nut loose with a long breaker bar. Remove the three bolts behind the knuckle and tap the hub out. Slide the axle shaft out, remove the U-joint clips and press out the old joint. Press in the new joint, being careful not to disturb the needle bearings, then refit the clips, shaft, hub and brakes. Anti-seize the hub, torque everything to spec, and expect the other side to need the same soon.
repairs.tools: 36 mm socket · big breaker bar · 13 mm sockets · press (strongly preferred) · snap-ring pliers · anti-seize · torque wrench.

parts.name: Crown Automotive 8126638SP heavy-duty front axle U-joint, YJ/TJ/JK

repairs.title: Stop the rear main seal leak
repairs.cost: Seal kit plus oil-pan gasket; labor-heavy if paid for
repairs.symptoms: Oil dripping from the joint between engine and transmission and a wet bottom of the bellhousing. Rule out the valve cover and oil-filter adapter gasket first, because oil runs downhill.
repairs.fix: Clean the area and confirm the source. The seal is reached from below, which means dropping the oil pan. OffroadXtreme notes that on a TJ this can mean lowering the front axle to get the pan out. With the pan off, replace the seal following the kit's instructions and the factory manual's torque specs, then refit the pan with a new gasket and refill the oil. Do the oil-filter adapter O-rings while you're under there.
repairs.tools: Jack stands and floor jack (to lower the front axle if needed) · torque wrench · RTV per the factory manual · drain pan · factory service manual.

parts.name: Crankshaft rear main seal kit (5018594AA), 2000–06 4.0 L TJ

faq.q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
faq.a: The LJ uses the TJ's axles, flares and suspension, so the TJ answer applies: Four Wheel Trends puts the stock-suspension limit at about a 31x10.50, which may still rub at full flex until you add a washer or two to the steering stops. Jeep itself sent the Rubicon Unlimited out on LT245/75R16 (about 31-inch) tires at stock height. For 33s, plan on a lift; Quadratec's buyer's guide pairs 33s with a 3-inch-class suspension lift.

faq.q: What's the difference between an LJ and a TJ?
faq.a: The LJ has 10 more inches of wheelbase (103.4 in against 93.4 in), is about 15 inches longer overall, and has 2 more inches of rear legroom and 13 more inches of cargo length. It tows 3,500 lb instead of 2,000. Every LJ also got a Dana 44 rear axle (limited-slip on standard models, locking on the Rubicon), which many short TJs lacked.

Jalopnik's tally from forum and sales data puts it at about 47,000 across 2004–2006, roughly 20 percent of Wrangler sales in that period. Driving Line says a little over 46,000, fewer than 13,000 of them Rubicons. The 2005 Sahara Edition Unlimited Rubicon was a numbered run of 1,000.

faq.q: Why are LJs so expensive now?
faq.a: There's never been a replacement. It's the only factory Wrangler with two doors, a long wheelbase, coil springs and the 4.0 straight six, and the Rubicon version adds lockers at both ends. Hagerty says late TJs, 'especially the Unlimited Rubicon,' have been the priciest TJs on the market.

faq.q: Which years and drivetrains should I look for?
faq.a: 2005–06 brought the NSG370 six-speed manual. Those years also need the OPDA checked. The 2005–06 Rubicon Unlimited is the one with front and rear Dana 44s, air lockers and the 4:1 Rock-Trac. A 2004 or non-Rubicon LJ still has the Dana 44 rear and is a better starting point for a build than a Dana 35 TJ.
Jeep rated the LJ at 3,500 lb, against 2,000 lb for the short-wheelbase TJ.

Quadratec's factory-based chart gives the 4.0 6 qt of 10W-30 with a filter and 10.5 qt of coolant. The 42RLE takes ATF+4, 4 qt at a service fill. The NSG370 takes 3.17 pints. The NV231 takes 2.2 pints and the NV241 Rock-Trac 4.2 pints of ATF+4. The Dana 30 takes 2.5 pints and a Dana 44 4.0 pints of GL-5 80W-90 or 75W-140 synthetic. Rubicons specify 75W-140 synthetic, and a Trac-Lok rear needs 4 oz of limited-slip additive.

The oil pump drive assembly on 2005–06 4.0 engines can wear. The warning sign owners describe is a 'laughing monkey' noise, and if it's ignored the engine can be damaged. Replacements with a relocated seal are cheap; the indexing to keep the cam sensor in sync is the fiddly part.

faq.q: What fuel economy and range should I expect?
faq.a: Jeep's 2005–06 TJ spec sheet originally listed 16/20 mpg (city/highway) for the 4.0 with either transmission, on the short-wheelbase truck. EPA's revised figures on fueleconomy.gov are lower: 13/16 for the automatic and 13/17 for the six-speed. The LJ carries a 19-gallon tank (Jeep's 2004½ spec sheet). Bigger tires, a lift and a roof load cost several mpg.

faq.q: What about the low belly and the rear overhang?
faq.a: Jalopnik flags both. The departure angle is 27.7 degrees, and the transfer-case skid hangs low, so a high-clearance or 'tummy tuck' skid is a common first mod. Rough Country's 1126 is listed for 2003–06 TJ and Unlimited.

faq.q: Do I need a slip-yoke eliminator if I lift it?
faq.a: Quadratec says lift-kit makers strongly recommend an SYE and a CV driveshaft above 2 inches of lift, and treat it as required at 4 inches or more, to cure vibration and stop the slip yoke pulling out of the transfer case.

mods.why: The LJ's low transfer-case skid is the first thing to drag. A high-clearance skid tucks it up into the frame.

who.name: Rough Country 1126 high-clearance skid, 2003–06 TJ & Unlimited (Quadratec)

mods.why: 2–4 inches clears 33s. Above 2 inches, budget for an adjustable track bar, alignment correction and an SYE with a CV driveshaft.
Non-Rubicon LJs have only a rear limited slip. Selectable lockers turn an LJ Sport into most of a Rubicon.
The long rear overhang and the plastic corners are what get hurt. Steel rear corners and rocker sliders are standard trail kit.
Rust Buster sells bolt-up-and-weld replacement sections for the TJ's known rot zones.
Bigger tires bend the Dana 30 front tubes first. Trusses and diff guards are cheap insurance.

baseline_service.intro: Assume nothing has been done. Even a low-mile LJ is now 20 years old, so rubber, coolant and gear oil have aged regardless of mileage. On 2005–06 trucks, put the OPDA at the top of the list. On every LJ, put the frame inspection there too, before you spend a cent on mods.
